title: Quantum-ETH hardness of cryptographic-factor GapSVP
formal:
Does the quantum Exponential Time Hypothesis defined below imply that, for some fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is no bounded-error uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm for Euclidean
\[\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k},\qquad \gamma_k(n)=n^{3/2+1/k}?\]
Equivalently, the target is the conditional assertion
\[\mathrm{QETH}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\operatorname{GapSVP}_{\gamma_k}\notin\mathrm{PromiseBQP}.\]
The source asks for hardness at \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) under a standard complexity assumption, without selecting that assumption. This card explicitly selects quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT; it is an editorial variant of that research direction, not a claim that the source stated this particular implication.
why: This question asks whether a familiar quantum satisfiability assumption can support hardness of lattice approximation at a scale relevant to worst-case-to-average-case cryptographic reductions. That scale is much larger than constant-factor approximation, and hardness at a small factor does not automatically persist as the promise gap grows. A proof would connect lattice-based security foundations to a separate complexity assumption while addressing quantum algorithms explicitly.
status_note: Bennett’s January 2023 Definition 1.1, Section 4.1 and Open Problem 4.11, Chia–Chou–Zhang–Zhang’s ECCC revision Definition 4.25, Hecht–Safra’s Theorems 1.1–1.2, and Wan arXiv:2603.27398v3 Theorems 1.3/1.8 and surrounding scope were read on 2026-09-14. The recent results concern other norms or constant factors, and the Euclidean preprint proof was not independently verified. A bounded later-work search found no matching hardness theorem or algorithm for the selected cryptographic-factor implication. Quantum ETH is an explicitly chosen assumption variant of the source’s broader question; current source-open status does not assert that this particular implication was posed verbatim by Bennett.

sentences: The target is a conditional quantum lower bound for the Euclidean gap version of the shortest vector problem.
The approximation gap grows as dimension to the power three halves plus a fixed positive increment.
The card explicitly chooses the quantum exponential-time hypothesis for classical 3-SAT as its starting assumption.
It asks to exclude every bounded-error uniform quantum algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the full binary input length.
Recent constant-factor or different-norm hardness results do not establish this cryptographically relevant approximation regime.

definitions:
An instance consists of an integer \(n\ge1\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational threshold \(r\). The columns of \(B\) form a full-rank lattice basis. Its lattice and shortest-vector length are
\[\mathcal L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\},\qquad \lambda_1(B)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2,\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum exists and is positive for a nonsingular basis. No ideal-lattice, module-lattice, random-lattice or special-basis promise is imposed.

The promise problem has YES instances with \(\lambda_1(B)\le r\) and NO instances with \(\lambda_1(B)>\gamma_k(n)r\). Either condition is promised. For \(r<\lambda_1(B)\le\gamma_k(n)r\), either answer is allowed. This preserves the source’s strict inequality on the NO side. The task is deciding the promise, not outputting a short vector. The dimension in the approximation factor is \(n\), not the bit length of the matrix entries.

Use a binary encoding of \(n\), the matrix entries and \(r\), each rational represented by its signed reduced numerator and positive denominator, with self-delimiting lengths. Let \(L\) denote the total input bit length. A quantum polynomial-time solver is one finite uniform quantum algorithm, for the fixed chosen \(k\), which uses at most \(C(L+1)^a\) elementary operations for constants \(C,a\) on every branch, and returns the correct promise answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every YES and every NO instance. It must halt on all inputs within the time bound; malformed encodings, singular matrices and inputs outside the promise require no particular answer. This is the meaning of \(\mathrm{PromiseBQP}\) here. The program and polynomial may depend on \(k\), which is not an instance parameter.

For definiteness, uniform quantum computation uses a classical Turing controller, qubits initially in computational-basis states, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), and computational-basis measurements with the Born probabilities. On one qubit, \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\). The controlled-not gate maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Classical tape work, input reading, generation of gate instructions, gate applications and measurements are charged. The algorithm has no advice, external oracle, uncharged quantum state or postselection. Adaptive classical control and classical randomization obtained by measurement are allowed.

Quantum ETH in this card is a statement about classical Boolean satisfiability. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three signed Boolean variables. It is satisfiable if some assignment makes every clause true. Let \(N\) be its number of variables and \(s\) its binary encoding length. The assumption asserts that there exists \(\delta>0\) for which no uniform quantum algorithm decides satisfiability on every such formula, with error at most \(1/3\), in time \(C2^{\delta N}(s+1)^a\) for any fixed constants \(C,a\). Time is worst-case over inputs and measurement outcomes, in the same uniform quantum model. This uses the positive exponential-rate formulation of Definition 4.25 in the cited quantum complexity paper; it is not a hypothesis about the quantum satisfiability or local-Hamiltonian problem.

The exponent increment is fixed before instances or candidate solvers are considered. Writing it as \(1/k\) loses no existence case from an arbitrary constant \(\varepsilon>0\): choosing \(1/k\le\varepsilon\) only reduces the approximation factor, and a solver for the smaller factor also solves the larger-factor promise. The source’s alternative LWE target is not bundled into this card. No lattice-hardness or cryptographic-security assumption is available in addition to the stated quantum ETH premise.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed conditional assertion with these encodings, norm, approximation factor and uniform quantum model. A positive answer may assume quantum ETH as defined but must establish the claimed exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms, rather than assume hardness of GapSVP or LWE. It must obtain a fixed positive exponent increment and cover all promised rational-basis inputs. A lower bound only for classical algorithms, a constant-factor approximation problem, another norm, or exact SVP alone does not establish this target. Refuting the conditional assertion requires more than showing that one proposed reduction fails; likewise, refuting quantum ETH alone would make the implication vacuously true rather than false.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 4.11 distinguishes cryptographic approximation factors \(n^{3/2+\varepsilon}\) from smaller powers of the dimension and explicitly includes quantum algorithms. The named assumption is left open by the author; selecting the quantum 3-SAT hypothesis makes this card’s proof obligation concrete.

The cited quantum complexity paper defines a positive-exponential-rate quantum ETH for classical 3-SAT. Its assumption provides the premise used here, rather than an already known reduction to lattice problems.

The source surveys worst-case-to-average-case reductions connecting sufficiently large-factor Euclidean GapSVP hardness to appropriate Learning with Errors parameters. The direction relevant here is that an efficient LWE algorithm would give an efficient worst-case lattice algorithm; these reductions do not themselves derive lattice hardness from SAT hardness.

The source also describes certificate-based obstacles to ordinary NP-hardness at large approximation factors. This helps explain why a standard-assumption hardness theorem in the cryptographic range remains a distinct question from constant-factor NP-hardness.

Hecht and Safra’s STOC 2026 deterministic hardness results assume norms strictly above two. Their displayed factors and norm hypotheses do not establish the Euclidean, cryptographic-factor, quantum conclusion.

Wan’s July 2026 preprint claims deterministic Euclidean hardness within constant factors below \(\sqrt2\), as a special case of its Theorem 1.8. Even if that claim is verified, its approximation scale does not yield hardness for \(n^{3/2+1/k}\). It is recorded as a preprint claim, not as an independently verified resolution of the target.
